title: Half of global LNG capacity will sit in two countries by 2030, making Floating LNG the primary route to supply diversification
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues floating LNG has become the primary route to LNG supply diversification as half of global capacity concentrates in two countries by 2030 and Gulf disruption risks a ~70 mmtpa shortfall; FLNG costs now match onshore (Delfin at ~US$932/t), redeployment economics are compelling, but a single lease-and-operate provider (Golar LNG) constrains growth against an 80+ mmtpa pre-FID pipeline.

insights.claim: By 2030 roughly half of global LNG production capacity will sit in two countries.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Concentration raises importers' demand for diversified supply sources.
insights.quote: By 2030, roughly half of global LNG production capacity will sit in two countries.

insights.claim: Under an extended disruption to Gulf LNG supply, Wood Mackenzie estimates global LNG availability could run about 70 mmtpa below pre-conflict levels through 2035.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A sustained Gulf outage implies a large, multi-year LNG supply deficit supportive of prices and alternative supply.
insights.quote: global availability could run approximately 70 mmtpa below pre-conflict levels to 2035

insights.claim: Seven floating LNG projects sanctioned since 2023 add 18 mmtpa of new capacity across six countries, the market's most direct response to concentration and disruption risk.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: FLNG sanctioning momentum signals a growing equipment and services market.

insights.claim: Global FLNG capacity is projected to reach 37 mmtpa by 2031.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Defines the near-term scale of the FLNG segment.

insights.claim: FLNG's diversification case is geographic rather than volumetric: it is under 10% of new global liquefaction supply but opens resources conventional approaches cannot serve.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: FLNG value lies in unlocking frontier gas, not aggregate volumes.
insights.quote: The diversification case is geographic, not volumetric.

insights.claim: All proposed new LNG capacity in South America and West Africa is based on floating designs, and FLNG is frequently the only credible export route for Argentina's Vaca Muerta and West African gas provinces.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frontier gas monetisation in these regions depends on FLNG providers.
insights.quote: floating LNG is frequently the only credible export route

insights.claim: FLNG is a deliberate choice: economics can be tight versus low-cost modular onshore projects, but clear where it commercialises stranded or offshore resources with no alternative path to market.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Project selection should favour stranded/offshore resources over head-to-head onshore competition.
insights.quote: The question for developers is not whether the technology works, but where.

insights.claim: Fraser Carson says the cost gap between floating and onshore LNG has closed and FLNG now competes on merit in key locations, with cost and technology no longer the constraints.
insights.speaker: Fraser Carson
insights.so_what: FLNG is no longer a technology bet, lowering perceived project risk.
insights.quote: The cost gap with onshore has closed and floating LNG now competes on merit in the locations that matter.

insights.claim: Delfin LNG FLNG 1, sanctioned in June 2026 as the first US floating LNG export facility and at 4.4 mmtpa the largest single FLNG unit globally, came in at about US$932 per tonne, competitive with recent onshore US LNG FIDs.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Benchmark cost data point validates FLNG competitiveness in the US.
insights.locator: The economics confirm a cost threshold

insights.claim: FLNG conversions and standardised newbuilds can reach market at or below the sector benchmark of about US$950 to US$1,000 per tonne, and recent plant breakevens cluster between US$2.3 and US$4.6 per MMBtu.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Low breakevens imply resilient FLNG margins across price cycles.
insights.locator: The economics confirm a cost threshold

insights.claim: FLNG fleet utilisation averaged 88% in 2024 and 2025, above the 85% onshore average, though operating costs run structurally higher at about 3-5% of total capex per year.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Reliability is proven, but higher opex is a trade-off in project economics.
insights.locator: The economics confirm a cost threshold

insights.claim: Redeployment is FLNG's key differentiator: Hilli's redeployment costs to date are about US$350 million versus US$1.5-2 billion for a newbuild FLNG.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Redeployable assets lower capital at risk and improve returns versus fixed plants.
insights.quote: That difference funds a market entry, not a maintenance budget.

insights.claim: Golar LNG's Hilli recovered its roughly US$1.3 billion conversion cost over an eight-year Cameroon charter by 2023, generating about US$2.1 billion in tolling EBITDA.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track record demonstrates FLNG tolling payback and cash generation.

insights.claim: A roughly US$350 million redeployment and about one year of downtime unlocks a 20-year Hilli charter in Argentina with Southern Energy expected to produce about US$5.9 billion in contracted revenues.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Long-dated contracted revenue supports Golar LNG valuation visibility.
insights.quote: No fixed onshore plant can replicate that sequence.

insights.claim: Moving FLNG units within a 30-35 year hull life reduces exposure to upstream resource depletion and single-country risk.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Mobility lowers stranded-asset and sovereign risk relative to onshore plants.

insights.claim: Of 15 operational and under-construction FLNGs, 12 are project-owned and three are lease-and-operate, all belonging to Golar LNG, which committed to a fourth vessel on a speculative basis in 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Golar LNG holds a monopoly position in FLNG-as-a-service.

insights.claim: Fraser Carson notes one company provides FLNG as a service to the entire global market against a pre-FID pipeline of over 80 mmtpa, so growth hinges on commercial structures catching up.
insights.speaker: Fraser Carson
insights.so_what: Supply-constrained lease market supports pricing power for the incumbent and opportunity for new entrants.
insights.quote: One company currently provides FLNG as a service to the entire global market.

insights.claim: The lease-and-operate model shifts construction and financing risk to the vessel owner, lowering the capital barrier for frontier producers lacking balance sheet for integrated projects.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Lessor model expands addressable market among smaller producers.

insights.claim: With over 80 mmtpa of FLNG proposals pre-FID and an additional 160 tcf of undeveloped upstream assets suited to FLNG, the opening for new FLNG-as-a-service entrants is substantial.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Signals a sizeable greenfield opportunity for new lessors, shipyards and infrastructure investors.
insights.quote: the opening for new entrants is substantial

insights.claim: Fraser Carson says seven FLNG projects sanctioned in three years, backed by infrastructure investors, IOCs and LNG traders, is not a technology bet.
insights.speaker: Fraser Carson
insights.so_what: Broad sponsor base indicates FLNG has matured into mainstream infrastructure.
